title.en: Getting Clean JSON Out of a Messy LLM Reply

description.en: Ask an LLM for JSON and you often get JSON wrapped in prose and code fences. Build the extractor that finds the first real JSON object in a chatty reply — a survival skill for every structured-output pipeline.

story_variants.en:
## "Return JSON" Is a Suggestion, Not a Guarantee

"You ask the model for JSON," Vaathiyaar chuckles, "and it says: *'Sure! Here you go:'* then a code fence, then the JSON, then *'Let me know if you need anything else!'* Your `json.loads` chokes on the friendly bits. So every structured-output pipeline in 2026 has a little **extractor** that fishes the real JSON object out of the chatter."

### Find the Braces

The robust-enough trick: locate the first `{`, then walk forward tracking brace **depth** — `+1` on `{`, `-1` on `}` — until depth returns to zero. That span is one complete JSON object, prose and code fences ignored.

```
reply = 'Sure! ```json {"ok": true} ``` Done'
        find first '{' ......^
        depth: { =1 ... } =0  -> stop
extracted -> '{"ok": true}'  -> json.loads -> {'ok': True}
```

### Why Depth, Not Just "Next }"

JSON nests: `{"a": {"b": 1}}`. Grabbing text up to the *first* `}` would cut it in half. Counting depth handles nesting correctly — the object ends only when every `{` has been matched by a `}`.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** never assume an LLM returns *only* what you asked for. Extract, then parse. Belt and suspenders keeps structured pipelines alive.

Today you implement `extract_json(reply)` — return the first balanced `{...}` substring from a messy reply (as a string).

explanation.en: The JSON object begins at the first opening brace
Track nesting: up on '{', down on '}'
Every brace matched — this is one complete object

instruction.en: Implement `extract_json(reply)` — pull the first complete JSON object out of a chatty reply. Find the first `{`, then scan forward tracking brace depth (`+1` on `{`, `-1` on `}`); when depth returns to 0 you've found the end. Return that `{...}` substring (as a string). Then print `extract_json('Sure! Here: {"ok": true, "n": {"x": 1}} — done')` (expected: `{"ok": true, "n": {"x": 1}}`).
